svg.aria-label: Diagram: the seven Google Cloud security baseline constraints enforced by default since May 2024, the five constraints worth adding on day one, why almost none of them can be rehearsed with dry-run mode, and the two one-way doors among them
svg.title: Day-one organization policies: what Google already enforces, what to add, and what cannot be taken back
svg.text: The first question is not which policies to set. It is which are already set.
Most day-one lists were written before May 2024. A modern organization starts most of the way there.
Already enforced — the security baseline
For every organization created on or after 3 May 2024.
iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation
iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload
iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts
iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains
essentialcontacts.managed.allowedContactDomains
compute.managed.restrictProtocolForwardingCreationForTypes
storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess
Four of these are the strongest items on any
conventional hardening list.
Worth adding — and deliberately short
Every extra constraint is a way to block a team
that cannot see why.
compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation
no permissive default network per project
compute.vmExternalIpAccess
a list, so it can start wide and narrow later
compute.requireOsLogin
SSH on IAM identities, not metadata keys
storage.publicAccessPrevention
the baseline covers uniform access, not exposure
sql.restrictPublicIp
Almost none of the ones you add can be rehearsed
Dry run supports custom constraints, managed constraints and four named legacy ones. Every constraint in the
right-hand box is a legacy managed constraint outside those four, so attempting a dry run returns an error.
So stage by scope instead: set each on one non-critical folder, watch, then move it up the hierarchy.
Two doors that close behind you
Uniform bucket-level access
cannot be disabled after 90 consecutive days on a bucket.
The policy stays reversible; the effect on each bucket does not.
Public access prevention
enforced at a bucket survives the org policy being removed. And
existing allUsers grants remain in place — merely overridden.
The order that survives contact
1. Read the effective policy. Find out what the baseline already gave you.
2. Set the cheap reversible ones first — skipDefaultNetworkCreation costs nothing and prevents a lot.
3. Stage anything with a blast radius, one folder at a time, since none of it can be dry-run.
4. Set the one-way doors last, deliberately, once the estate’s shape is known.
Leave domain-restricted sharing until the end. It is the day-one policy most likely to lock you out.
Your own organization principal set and Google Workspace ID are not automatically allowed, and Google warns it can
prevent its own service accounts from being granted the roles they need, causing certain actions to fail.
